import { Aside } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

<Aside type="caution" title="Superseded by the in-app Cupboard">
The hosted `papercuspai.com/marketplace` + `marketplace-api` (`:3057`)
design described below — including the §11.4 "live as of 2026-04-26"
claims, the `marketplace-api`/`marketplace-site` apps, the Gitea/OCI and
`tenantId`/`tenantSecret` ideas elsewhere in the spec, and the
`papercusp publish` / `papercusp install <name>@<ver>` CLI — has been
**superseded** by the in-app **Cupboard** (`apps/operator-public`,
`@papercusp/cupboard-worker` — Cloudflare Workers + D1). The
`marketplace-api`/`marketplace-site` apps are gone; the old
`apps/papercup` reference install is retired to `_retired/papercup/`.

The Cupboard is **one storefront with ten listing kinds**
(`LISTING_KINDS` in `apps/operator-public/src/db.ts`): `harness` →
join; `blueprint` → fork; `plugin`, `pack`, `knowledge-pack`, and
`template` → install; `app` → download or install; and `rubric`, `plan`,
and `recipe` → install through their self-describing stores. Two earlier
kind values survive only as normalized wire aliases for older clients
(`normalizeListingKind`): `tool-pack` → `pack` (the runtime-less
code-tool pack, briefly named `tool-pack` by migration 008 and renamed
back to `pack`) and `learning-pack` → `knowledge-pack` (migration 011).
Listings are keyed on the GitHub-backed project remote.

Instruction/judgment-carrying kinds (`knowledge-pack`, `blueprint`,
`rubric`, `plan`, `recipe`) publish as `pending` and are publicly invisible
until an operator approves them; the remaining kinds (`harness`, `plugin`,
`pack`, `template`, `app`) publish as `approved` immediately. A non-approved row is `not_found` to
everyone except its publisher. See `REVIEW_POLICY_KINDS` in
`apps/operator-public/src/routes/listings.ts`.

Auth is a GitHub bearer (validated against
`https://api.github.com/user`), **not** namespace OAuth +
Ed25519-server-signing as §11.6 describes; publisher trust is the
GitHub repo-permission signal plus an optional Ed25519 device-pubkey ↔
login attestation (gist-bound). The live route surface is broader than
just `/listings`: there is also the `/harnesses*` back-compat view
(`fixedKind: 'harness'`), the repo → harness binding lookup
(`GET /binding/:github_repository_id`), abuse reporting
(`POST /reports`), and an operator moderation surface (`/admin`, with a
publisher-pubkey ban-list). The publish path enforces private-repo
rejection, a 5/hr-per-user publish cap, and pubkey ban-list filtering.
See `apps/operator-public/README.md` and the route handlers under
`apps/operator-public/src/routes/`.

The sections below are **retained as design history**; treat the
namespace-policy / federation / SBOM / webhook material as aspirational,
not current behavior.
</Aside>

<p>
        A Papercusp install is distributable. The marketplace is a hosted catalog of harness installs (or plugins for installs), distributed as tarballs.
      </p>

      

### 11.1 Publish (with secret scrubbing)



      

```
# Inside an install directory:
papercusp publish

# Substrate runs:
# 1. Validate against the harness contract (4 roles + state schema + capabilities)
# 2. Run secret scrubber across all files (gitleaks regex set + custom patterns)
# 3. If secrets found:
#    - HARD BLOCK by default, list findings
#    - --acknowledge-secrets replaces them with ${SECRET_NAME} placeholders
# 4. Pack into a tarball (excludes node_modules, .git, .harness state, .env*)
# 5. Upload to the marketplace catalog
# 6. Register name + version in the registry
```



      <p>
        Secret scrubber rules borrow from <strong>gitleaks</strong> (regex set: AWS, GCP, GitHub PAT, Stripe, Anthropic `sk-ant-*`, OpenAI `sk-*`, Cloudflare `cfut_*`) plus harness-specific patterns (anything ending in `_KEY`, `_SECRET`, `_TOKEN`, `_PASSWORD` in env-shaped files).
      </p>

      

### 11.2 Install



      

```
# Pull a published install:
papercusp install habit-tracker@0.2.1

# Substrate:
# 1. Download tarball, verify signature
# 2. Show capability manifest, prompt user consent (§10.3)
# 3. Resolve any ${SECRET_NAME} placeholders by prompting
# 4. Apply DB migrations (plugin's Postgres schema)
# 5. Register routines, hooks, UI contributions
# 6. Save granted-capabilities.json
# Project mounted at ~/.papercusp/projects/habit-tracker/
```



      

### 11.3 Run



      

```
# In any project dir:
papercusp run

# Substrate boots:
# 1. Reads schema state (creates fresh if not present)
# 2. Loads installed plugins, applies their schemas
# 3. Loops: orchestrator tick → execute decision → repeat
# 4. Honors lifecycle hooks at each phase
# 5. Routine ticker runs in parallel for cron events
```



      

### 11.4 Live marketplace infrastructure



      <p>
        <strong>Historical (superseded — see banner at top):</strong> the

        <strong>papercuspai.com/marketplace</strong> (MVP, 2026-04-26) on the

        apps. It has been replaced by the Cupboard. The architecture below is
        kept for reference only. Original architecture:

```
papercuspai.com  (Cloudflare Pages — static Next.js export)
   │
   ├──> /  /marketplace/  /marketplace/[slug]/  /docs/
   │
   │ runtime fetch (CORS-allowed origin)
   ▼
api.papercuspai.com  (Cloudflare Tunnel — public ingress)
   │
   │ tunnel → cloudflared (token mode)
   │   tunnel UUID c53515b3-edfe-4e99-813b-e3916ae9d02c (papercupai-api)
   ▼
http://localhost:3057  (marketplace-api — Hono on Node, libs/papercusp/apps/marketplace-api)
   │
   │ filesystem read
   ▼
~/.papercusp/marketplace-storage/<slug>/<version>/
   ├── papercusp.json          (manifest)

   └── <slug>-<version>.tar.gz (the install)
```

      <h4>Two-base build pattern</h4>

      <p>
        Cloudflare Pages exports static HTML at build time, then the deployed bundle runs in browsers worldwide. Two API URLs are needed:
      </p>

      

```
# Build server-side (generateStaticParams) — uses BUILD_API_BASE
# Client bundle baked-in URL (runtime fetches) — uses NEXT_PUBLIC_API_BASE
BUILD_API_BASE=http://localhost:3057 \\
NEXT_PUBLIC_API_BASE=https://api.papercuspai.com \\
  npm --workspace @papercusp/marketplace-site run build
```



      <p>
        At build, generateStaticParams hits the local marketplace-api (faster, doesn't need DNS). The output static pages reference `https://api.papercuspai.com` for runtime fetches by browsers.
      </p>

      <h4>CORS allowlist (in marketplace-api)</h4>

      

```
https://papercuspai.com
https://www.papercuspai.com
*.pages.dev                       (Cloudflare Pages preview deploys)
http://localhost:3060             (local site dev)
http://localhost:3050             (papercup public site dev)
http://192.168.40.216:3060        (LAN dev)
```

### 11.5 Outstanding marketplace work



      <p>
        The §11.4 deployment is MVP. Production-grade requires:
      </p>

      <table>
        <thead><tr><th>Concern</th><th>Status</th><th>What's needed</th></tr></thead>
        <tbody>
          <tr><td><strong>Auth on publish</strong></td><td>⚠ Open (no auth)</td><td>GitHub OAuth + namespace claim. Publishing under `@user/name` requires proven ownership of the GitHub user/org. Squatting prevention.</td></tr>
          <tr><td><strong>Tarball storage</strong></td><td>⚠ Local FS</td><td>Move to Cloudflare R2 with signed download URLs so marketplace-api scales beyond one box. `storageRoot` field in `/catalog` response is already a hint at multi-backend support.</td></tr>
          <tr><td><strong>Tarball signing</strong></td><td>❌ Missing</td><td>Sign at publish with Ed25519 server key; verify at install. CLI rejects unsigned tarballs from untrusted sources.</td></tr>
          <tr><td><strong>Search + tags</strong></td><td>⚠ Client-side only</td><td>`/catalog` returns the full list; the site filters in-memory. Large catalogs (1k+) need server-side filtering — Typesense index, query API.</td></tr>
          <tr><td><strong>Stats</strong></td><td>❌ Missing</td><td>Download counts, popularity ranking, trending. Fed back to ranking on `/marketplace/`.</td></tr>
          <tr><td><strong>Author profiles + reviews</strong></td><td>❌ Missing</td><td>`/authors/[name]`, `/marketplace/[slug]#reviews`. Trust signals before install.</td></tr>
          <tr><td><strong>Update flow</strong></td><td>❌ Missing</td><td>`papercusp update &lt;name&gt;` — diff capabilities (prompt for new ones), run new migrations, version-pin previous in case of rollback. <strong>Spec'd in §11.7.</strong></td></tr>
          <tr><td><strong>Uninstall</strong></td><td>❌ Missing</td><td>No formal teardown of plugin schema, granted-capabilities, routines, registry entry. <strong>Spec'd in §11.8.</strong></td></tr>
          <tr><td><strong>Size / bandwidth quotas</strong></td><td>❌ Missing</td><td>Per-package size limits, per-publisher daily upload quota, per-IP throttling. <strong>Spec'd in §11.10.</strong></td></tr>
          <tr><td><strong>Catalog webhooks</strong></td><td>❌ Missing</td><td>CI / mirror / monitor notifications on `version.published` etc. <strong>Spec'd in §11.11.</strong></td></tr>
          <tr><td><strong>Offline install</strong></td><td>❌ Missing</td><td>`papercusp pack` for vendored mirrors; `file://` registry URLs. <strong>Spec'd in §11.12.</strong></td></tr>
          <tr><td><strong>Multi-registry resolution</strong></td><td>❌ Missing</td><td>Scope-based routing across multiple registries; no automatic fallback. <strong>Spec'd in §11.13.</strong></td></tr>
          <tr><td><strong>Supply chain attestation</strong></td><td>❌ Missing (optional in v1.0)</td><td>SPDX / CycloneDX SBOMs at publish; CVE scanning via osv.dev. <strong>Spec'd in §11.14.</strong></td></tr>
        </tbody>
      </table>

      

### 11.6 Authorization & namespace policy



      <p>
        The marketplace is the trust boundary. The spec commits to one namespace policy, two trust tiers, and an explicit federation stance.
      </p>

      <h4>Namespace policy</h4>

      <p>
        Names are scoped: <code>@&lt;owner&gt;/&lt;package&gt;</code>, where `owner` is a verified GitHub user or org. Examples: `@papercusp/coding-project`, `@owner/habit-tracker`, `@anthropic-team/internal-roles`.
      </p>

      <ul>
        <li>To publish under `@owner/foo`, the publisher must prove ownership of GitHub user `owner` via OAuth at publish time. The marketplace verifies via GitHub's token-introspection API and stores the verified login on the package row (`publishedBy: 'owner'`).</li>
        <li><strong>No bare names.</strong> `papercusp install foo` is rejected; the user must spell the full namespace. This eliminates a whole class of typo-squatting.</li>
        <li><strong>Reserved namespaces:</strong> `@papercusp/*` for first-party packages, gated by a hard-coded membership list (currently: members of the <strong>`Papercusp` GitHub organization</strong> — see the canonical identity note below; `papercupai` is a person, not an org, and cannot be an org-membership target). Plus reserved single-word namespaces blocked from claim: `examples`, `test`, `internal`, `system`, `admin`, `root`, `public`, `private`, `papercup`, `cli`, `sdk`, `api`, `ui` — these are reserved at the marketplace server. New first-party reservations are added by patch-version bumps to the spec.</li>
        <li><strong>`publishedBy` is immutable.</strong> The verified GitHub login stamped on a published version is permanent for that row, even if the user later renames their GitHub account. The marketplace tracks renames separately (a `github_login_rename` audit table) so the spec can answer "who originally published this?" deterministically. Renames don't affect ownership of packages — those follow the GitHub identity (`user.id`, not `user.login`).</li>
        <li><strong>Namespace transfer.</strong> An owner can transfer `@me/foo` to `@you/foo` via `papercusp transfer @me/foo @you`. Both parties must approve via OAuth-signed challenges within 7 days; on completion, the marketplace inserts a `namespace_transfers` audit row with both verified logins, and future publishes go to the new owner. Existing version rows keep their `publishedBy` (immutable). The CLI shows "transferred from @me to @you on `<date>`" on the package detail page.</li>
      </ul>

      <blockquote>
        <p>
          <strong>Canonical GitHub identity (read this once, link to it elsewhere — don't re-describe it):</strong>{' '}
          <code>papercupai</code> is a GitHub <strong>User</strong> account (created 2026-04-25) — the maintainer's personal admin login,
          used to sign in and administer the project. <code>Papercusp</code> is a separate GitHub <strong>Organization</strong>
          (created 2026-05-28) that owns the canonical repositories (`Papercusp/papercup`, `Papercusp/papercusp-registry`, …);
          <code>papercupai</code> has active admin membership in it. The two are related but distinct identities — a GitHub
          user cannot itself be an "org", so any check or doc that talks about "the <code>papercupai</code> org" is describing
          an identity that doesn't exist and is a drift bug (see WI-4978). When first-party/org-membership semantics are meant,
          the org is always <code>Papercusp</code>; when a personal-account/admin-login is meant, it's <code>papercupai</code>.
        </p>
      </blockquote>

      <h4>Two trust tiers</h4>

      <table>
        <thead><tr><th>Tier</th><th>Who's in it</th><th>What changes</th></tr></thead>
        <tbody>
          <tr>
            <td><strong>Verified</strong></td><td>Packages whose publisher has confirmed email + linked GitHub identity + signed Ed25519 signature on every version.</td>
            <td>Shows a checkmark badge in the marketplace UI; CLI doesn't warn at install time.</td>
          </tr>
          <tr>
            <td><strong>Unverified</strong></td>
            <td>Packages with valid namespace ownership but no signature, OR signed with a key the marketplace hasn't seen before.</td>
            <td>CLI prints a warning at install time: `WARNING: @user/foo is unverified (no signature). Continue? [y/N]`</td>
          </tr>
        </tbody>
      </table>

      <h4>Federation</h4>

      <p>
        <strong>papercuspai.com is the canonical marketplace</strong> for the open standard. Other marketplaces can exist (private, enterprise, regional), but the CLI defaults to <code>https://api.papercuspai.com</code> and the spec doesn't define cross-registry resolution. Operators wanting an alternate marketplace use <code>papercusp config set registry &lt;url&gt;</code>; install commands then resolve against that registry alone. <strong>No automatic fallback chain</strong> — that's a vector for attacker-controlled mirrors to inject impostor packages.
      </p>

      

### 11.7 Update flow



      <p>
        Updating a plugin is structurally different from a fresh install: the substrate has to compare two manifests and reason about migration ordering.
      </p>

      ```
$ papercusp update @owner/shareholder-briefings

Currently installed: 1.0.4
Latest available:    1.2.0

Capability changes:
  + secrets:read:OPENAI_API_KEY        (new)
  + http:fetch:openai.com              (new)
  - secrets:read:DALL_E_KEY            (no longer requested; revoked)

Migrations to apply:
  002_add_summary_table.sql
  003_index_message_recipients.sql

Routine changes:
  ~ weekly-briefings: cron changed from '0 9 * * MON' to '0 9 * * MON,THU'
  + daily-cost-report: NEW (cron '0 8 * * *')

Approve new capabilities? [y/N/per-capability]: y
Apply migrations? [y/N]: y
Updating ... done. Pinned old version 1.0.4 at ~/.papercusp/installed/@owner/shareholder-briefings/.snapshots/1.0.4/
```

      <p>The update flow is governed by these rules:</p>

      <ul>
        <li><strong>Capability diff prompts only for additions.</strong> Removed capabilities are auto-revoked; previously-granted ones aren't re-asked.</li>
        <li><strong>Migrations apply in declared order.</strong> Plugin manifest lists migration files in `schema[]` (already spec'd in §10.1). The substrate runs only the ones higher than the install's current `applied_migration_index`.</li>
        <li><strong>Old version is snapshotted</strong> to <code>.snapshots/&lt;old-version&gt;/</code> before the new files are unpacked. Includes the granted-capabilities.json, all schema dumps for plugin's tables, and the manifest. <strong>Rollback is not automatic</strong> (down-migrations are unsafe in general), but the snapshot lets `papercusp rollback &lt;name&gt;` re-mount the old version's files; the user is responsible for any DB rollback.</li>
        <li><strong>Routines reconcile.</strong> Renamed/removed routines from the old version are deleted from `routines` table; new ones inserted; modified ones updated in place.</li>
        <li><strong>Active state preserved.</strong> Plugin's data (Postgres tables, granted-capabilities) is never touched by update. Only the code + manifest are replaced.</li>
      </ul>

      

### 11.8 Uninstall flow



      <p>
        The default uninstall is conservative: stop the code, leave the data.
      </p>

      ```
$ papercusp uninstall @owner/shareholder-briefings

Will remove:
  - 4 routines (weekly-briefings, daily-cost-report, ...)
  - Plugin code: ~/.papercusp/installed/@owner/shareholder-briefings/
  - Granted capabilities
  - Registry entry
  - Hook subscriptions
  - UI contributions (1 sidebar item, 1 dashboard tab)

Will KEEP (use --purge-data to also remove):
  - Postgres schema "briefings" (4 tables, ~12,300 rows)
  - Plugin's secrets references (the secrets themselves are not deleted from the secret store)

Continue? [y/N]: y
Uninstalled. Run with --purge-data later if you want to reclaim DB space.
```

      <p>
        Why not auto-drop the schema? Because uninstall is often "I want to try a different version" or "this plugin is buggy, let me reinstall". Losing the data is a one-way action; preserving it is reversible. Users can `--purge-data` explicitly when they truly want a clean slate.
      </p>

      <p>
        After uninstall:
      </p>

      <ul>
        <li>The plugin's code is gone; no further routine fires; no further hook handlers run.</li>
        <li>The plugin's schema persists; another install of the same plugin (any version) can re-attach to it.</li>
        <li>Reference to the schema from `routines` and `granted_capabilities` tables is deleted; those rows are gone.</li>
        <li>The `audit.uninstalls` table records: plugin name, version, time, whether `--purge-data` was used.</li>
      </ul>

      <p>
        <strong>Reinstall after uninstall.</strong> If the user later runs `papercusp install &lt;same-name&gt;` and the plugin's schema still exists, the install flow detects it and prompts: "Schema 'briefings' already exists with 12,300 rows. Adopt existing data, or DROP and start fresh? [adopt/drop]". Default is `adopt`. The plugin's migrations resume from `applied_migration_index` recorded in the substrate's `installed_plugins` table.
      </p>

      

### 11.9 Package retraction (server-side)



      <p>
        Sometimes a published package must be pulled from circulation —
        leaked credentials, malicious code, legal request, namespace
        ownership transfer. Retraction is server-side only; once a tarball
        is on a user's machine, the substrate can't reach in and remove it.
      </p>

      <h4>Retraction levels</h4>

      <table>
        <thead><tr><th>Level</th><th>Effect on marketplace</th><th>Effect on installed users</th></tr></thead>
        <tbody>
          <tr>
            <td><strong>Deprecated</strong></td>
            <td>Listed with a "Deprecated" banner. New `papercusp install` shows a warning but proceeds. New version uploads still allowed.</td>
            <td>None — existing installs keep running. Updates show "the maintainer marked this package deprecated; consider an alternative" warning.</td>
          </tr>
          <tr>
            <td><strong>Yanked</strong></td>
            <td>Specific version hidden from listing pages. New installs of that version fail with "yanked: &lt;reason&gt;". Other versions of the same package unaffected.</td>
            <td>None automatically. CLI `papercusp doctor` reports "you have a yanked version installed; consider updating".</td>
          </tr>
          <tr>
            <td><strong>Withdrawn</strong></td>
            <td>Entire package hidden from listing. New installs at any version fail. Tarballs still downloadable by direct URL (with a 410 Gone status pending grace period).</td>
            <td>Substrate emits a `package.withdrawn` notification at next routine fire; user sees an alert in the UI. Code keeps running until the user acts.</td>
          </tr>
          <tr>
            <td><strong>Quarantined</strong> (security)</td>
            <td>Same as Withdrawn, plus tarball returns 410 immediately (no grace period).</td>
            <td>Substrate <strong>auto-pauses all routines</strong> from the quarantined package on next refresh from the catalog. Code is not executed; UI shows "this plugin has been quarantined for security reasons" prominently. User must explicitly `papercusp uninstall` (or `papercusp force-resume` if they accept the risk).</td>
          </tr>
        </tbody>
      </table>

      <h4>Who can retract</h4>

      <ul>
        <li><strong>Deprecate / yank</strong> — the package owner (verified GitHub identity per §11.6) at any time, via `papercusp deprecate` / `papercusp yank`.</li>
        <li><strong>Withdraw</strong> — the package owner, OR the marketplace operator (papercuspai.com admins) for ToS violations.</li>
        <li><strong>Quarantine</strong> — only the marketplace operator. Reserved for active security incidents (leaked credentials in a tarball, confirmed malware, court order). Reason is published to a public audit log at `papercuspai.com/security/quarantines`.</li>
      </ul>

      <h4>Catalog-poll behavior</h4>

      <p>
        The substrate polls the catalog at most once per hour (default;
        configurable, but never less than once per day). Each installed plugin
        is checked for retraction status; quarantined ones trigger immediate
        pause. The substrate does <strong>not</strong> auto-update plugins —
        it only acts on explicit retraction signals.
      </p>

      <p>
        Tarballs cached at <code>~/.papercusp/cache/tarballs/&lt;slug&gt;-&lt;version&gt;.tar.gz</code>
        are kept regardless of retraction state — useful for forensic
        analysis after a security event.
      </p>

      <h4>Quarantine appeal process</h4>

      <p>
        Quarantines are operator decisions; they have a defined appeal path so
        owners aren't permanently silenced without recourse:
      </p>

      <ol>
        <li>Owner emails `appeals@papercuspai.com` (or files a GitHub issue against `papercupai/marketplace-appeals`) within 30 days.</li>
        <li>Operator publishes the appeal + their original quarantine reasoning to the public audit log within 7 days.</li>
        <li>Resolution is one of two outcomes. <strong>Upheld:</strong> quarantine stays; owner can re-publish at a new namespace if it was a false-positive on identity, or re-publish a fixed version if it was a content issue. <strong>Reversed:</strong> quarantine downgraded to "withdrawn" (less severe); owner may un-withdraw within 7 days. The audit log records the reversal.</li>
        <li>Substrate-side: when a quarantine is reversed, installs that auto-paused on quarantine see a `package.unquarantined` event; routines remain paused (user must explicitly resume) but the UI alert clears.</li>
      </ol>

      

### 11.10 Package size & bandwidth quotas



      <p>
        The marketplace must enforce limits to prevent abuse: oversized
        tarballs filling storage, runaway publishing draining the publisher's
        own quota, malicious downloaders fetching high-bandwidth tarballs in
        loops to inflate operator costs.
      </p>

      <h4>Per-package limits</h4>

      <ul>
        <li><strong>Tarball size:</strong> 50 MB hard limit per version. Larger packages must split — typical mature plugins (papercup-org, sheets-clone) are well under 1 MB compressed.</li>
        <li><strong>Manifest size:</strong> 64 KB. Forces author to use compact JSON, not bundled assets.</li>
        <li><strong>README size:</strong> 256 KB. Forces docs to live elsewhere (linked from the package's `homepage`) for any non-trivial documentation.</li>
        <li><strong>Total versions per slug:</strong> unlimited (kept as audit trail), but only the latest 100 surface in the catalog UI by default.</li>
      </ul>

      <h4>Per-publisher quotas</h4>

      <ul>
        <li><strong>Publishes per day:</strong> 50 versions across all the publisher's packages, total. Resets at UTC rollover.</li>
        <li><strong>Aggregate storage:</strong> 1 GB total across all versions of all packages owned by the publisher. Yanked + withdrawn versions still count until purged.</li>
        <li><strong>Higher quotas</strong> available on operator request (no formal SLA; for first-party packages and verified high-value contributors).</li>
      </ul>

      <h4>Per-IP download throttling</h4>

      <p>
        At the API edge:
      </p>

      <ul>
        <li>`GET /catalog` and read endpoints: 600 requests/minute/IP (matches an internal admin's tunneled mirror; calibrated to allow a busy CI but reject scrapers).</li>
        <li>`GET /download/:slug/:version`: 60 tarballs/hour/IP. Caches don't count (signed R2 URLs, see §11.5 outstanding work).</li>
        <li>`POST /publish/:slug/:version`: 5/minute/authenticated user. Prevents accidental loops.</li>
      </ul>

      <p>
        Throttle violations return HTTP 429 with `Retry-After` header. CI
        clients that hit the limit should back off; their `papercusp.config.json`
        can declare a sustained-rate token from the operator.
      </p>

      

### 11.11 Catalog webhooks for CI/CD



      <p>
        Operators want to wire their CI pipelines to publish on tag, mirrors
        want to pull on new versions, listeners want notifications. The
        marketplace exposes outbound webhooks for catalog events.
      </p>

      <h4>Subscribe to catalog events</h4>

      ```typescript
// Authenticated; only the namespace owner can subscribe to events for that namespace.
POST /v1/webhooks
{
  "owner": "@owner",                           // namespace this webhook subscribes to
  "url": "https://hooks.example.com/papercusp",
  "events": ["version.published", "version.yanked", "package.withdrawn"],
  "secret": "<32-byte-base64-shared-secret>" // for HMAC-SHA-256 signing
}
```

      <h4>Event payloads</h4>

      <p>
        Each delivery is an HTTP POST with header `X-Papercusp-Signature: sha256=<hex>` (HMAC of body using the subscription's secret) and a JSON body:
      </p>

      ```json
{
  "id": "wh_evt_01J6...",                    // unique per delivery, for dedup
  "event": "version.published",
  "ts": 1777286087000,
  "deliveryAttempt": 1,
  "data": {
    "slug": "@owner/habit-tracker",
    "version": "1.2.0",
    "publishedBy": "owner",
    "publishedAt": "2026-04-27T14:34:47Z",
    "tarballSha256": "abc123...",
    "manifestUrl": "https://api.papercuspai.com/catalog/@owner/habit-tracker/1.2.0"
  }
}
```

      <h4>Delivery semantics</h4>

      <ul>
        <li><strong>At-least-once delivery.</strong> Same `id` may be delivered more than once on retry. Receivers must dedup by `id`.</li>
        <li><strong>Retry schedule:</strong> exponential backoff. Attempts at 0s, 30s, 5min, 1hr, 6hr, 24hr; after 6 attempts (≈31 hours), the delivery is dropped. Subscribers see drops in `papercusp webhooks history`.</li>
        <li><strong>Endpoint must respond with 2xx within 10 seconds.</strong> Slower or non-2xx → retry per schedule.</li>
        <li><strong>Webhook age limit:</strong> 90 days inactive (no successful delivery) auto-disables the subscription; owner gets one email reminder before disable.</li>
      </ul>

      <h4>Cross-event vs single-event subscriptions</h4>

      <p>
        Operators can subscribe to the entire catalog (`owner: "*"` requires
        operator role) — used by monitoring dashboards and the public audit log.
      </p>

      

### 11.12 Offline / vendored install



      <p>
        Enterprise and air-gapped environments can't reach
        `api.papercuspai.com`. The substrate supports local mirroring:
      </p>

      <h4>Vendoring with `papercusp pack`</h4>

      ```
$ papercusp pack @owner/habit-tracker @owner/habit-tracker@1.2.0 \
    --output ./vendored/

Wrote:
  ./vendored/@owner/habit-tracker/1.2.0/papercusp.json
  ./vendored/@owner/habit-tracker/1.2.0/README.md
  ./vendored/@owner/habit-tracker/1.2.0/habit-tracker-1.2.0.tar.gz
  ./vendored/@owner/habit-tracker/1.2.0/habit-tracker-1.2.0.tar.gz.sig
  ./vendored/marketplace.pub                              ← public key for verification
  ./vendored/index.json                                   ← catalog snapshot

Total: 1.1 MB across 5 files.
```

      <p>
        The `vendored/` directory is a self-contained mirror. Drop it on a
        USB drive, into S3, or commit to git. The receiving substrate is
        configured to use it as the registry.
      </p>

      <h4>Configuring the substrate to use a vendored mirror</h4>

      ```
papercusp config set registry file:///mnt/usb/vendored/
# or
papercusp config set registry https://internal-mirror.example.com/papercusp/
# or for a specific install:
papercusp install --registry file:///mnt/usb/vendored/ @owner/habit-tracker
```

      <p>
        File-based registries use the same JSON-blob layout that
        `papercuspai.com` serves. The substrate's resolver doesn't care whether
        it reads from HTTP or filesystem — only the URL scheme switches.
      </p>

      <h4>Limitations of offline mode</h4>

      <ul>
        <li>No version-discovery beyond what's in the local index — newer versions of installed plugins won't auto-detect until the mirror is refreshed.</li>
        <li>Retraction signals (§11.9) don't propagate without a live registry. Offline operators must subscribe to a webhook (§11.11) or refresh the mirror manually.</li>
        <li>Stats (downloads, popularity) are not tracked offline.</li>
      </ul>

      

### 11.13 Mirror & fallback registry resolution



      <p>
        Some operators want to fall back to papercuspai.com for packages not
        in their internal mirror. The spec keeps this <strong>opt-in and
        explicit</strong>; no automatic fallback chain (per §11.6).
      </p>

      <h4>Multi-registry config</h4>

      ```
# In ~/.papercusp/config.json:
{
  "registries": [
    { "url": "https://internal.example.com/papercusp/", "scope": "@example/*" },
    { "url": "https://api.papercuspai.com",              "scope": "*",          "trustOnFail": false }
  ]
}
```

      <ul>
        <li><strong>Scope-based routing.</strong> First match wins. `@example/foo` always resolves to internal; `@owner/foo` resolves to papercuspai.com.</li>
        <li><strong>Explicit fallback only.</strong> No registry can claim packages it doesn't have a scope match for. The CLI errors with "no registry covers @other/foo" rather than searching all configured registries.</li>
        <li><strong>`trustOnFail: false`</strong> (default): if a higher-priority registry is unreachable, the install fails — never silently falls through to a lower-priority one. Setting `true` requires explicit operator opt-in (logged in audit).</li>
      </ul>

      <p>
        This pattern is borrowed from `pip` and `cargo` after they had to
        retroactively retrofit fallback safety. Building it in from day 1
        avoids the "what registry does my package come from?" supply-chain
        confusion.
      </p>

      

### 11.14 Supply chain attestation (SBOM, optional)



      <p>
        Verified packages (per §11.6) may optionally publish a
        <strong>Software Bill of Materials</strong> at publish time. The
        marketplace stores it as a separate attestation, displays it on the
        detail page, and exposes it via the API.
      </p>

      <h4>Attestation format</h4>

      <p>
        The substrate accepts SBOMs in <strong>SPDX 2.3</strong> or
        <strong>CycloneDX 1.5</strong> JSON formats — both widely-supported
        open standards. Authors can generate them via existing tools
        (`syft scan dir:.`, `cdxgen .`) and submit at publish time:
      </p>

      ```
$ papercusp publish --sbom ./sbom.spdx.json

Validated against SPDX 2.3 schema. Found 47 dependencies, 0 vulnerabilities.
Attestation published. Detail page at https://papercuspai.com/marketplace/@owner/foo/1.2.0/sbom
```

      <h4>What it enables</h4>

      <ul>
        <li><strong>Vulnerability lookup.</strong> The marketplace scans new SBOMs against public CVE databases (osv.dev) and flags vulnerable dependencies on the detail page. Operators can subscribe to webhooks for "any installed plugin gets a new CVE matched".</li>
        <li><strong>Reproducibility verification.</strong> Authors can publish source location for each dependency; sceptics can verify the published tarball was actually built from those sources.</li>
        <li><strong>Compliance.</strong> Enterprise / regulated industries (healthcare, finance) can require all installed plugins to have published SBOMs.</li>
      </ul>

      <h4>Discoverability</h4>

      <p>
        Detail page surfaces:
      </p>

      <ul>
        <li>"Has SBOM" badge (with link to formatted SBOM viewer at `/marketplace/@owner/foo/1.2.0/sbom`).</li>
        <li>"N known vulnerabilities" if any deps have unpatched CVEs (linked to the specific advisories).</li>
        <li>SBOM diff between versions (helpful for reviewers to see new dependencies).</li>
      </ul>

      <p>
        SBOMs are <strong>optional in v1.0</strong>. Mandatory SBOMs are a
        v2.0 question pending operator feedback — too aggressive for the
        first version, but enterprises will likely require them. Verified
        packages without SBOMs aren't penalized; they just don't get the
        SBOM badge.
      </p>
